name: Paper Animation
tagline: Browser tool that turns a still image or a short phrase into paper-craft style animated videos and GIFs.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: This is a narrow effects tool, and narrow effects tools are exactly what coding agents are good at. If the paper-craft look is deterministic compositing, layered cutouts, drop shadows, paper grain, fold creases, a canvas or shader pipeline plus ffmpeg gets you a convincing local clone in a sitting. If the look actually comes from a generative video model, your DIY version is a form that posts to someone else's API and you pay per render either way, which is a thinner win. The gap in both cases is taste: the presets, the easing curves, and the paper textures are the product, and a one-shot build gives you one mediocre preset instead of several good ones. Build it if you want unlimited renders of one look you control; pay if you want the look to be good without you art-directing it.
coreLoopDIY: A local web page where you drop an image or type a phrase, pick a paper-cutout preset, and get an MP4 and GIF rendered by a canvas animation piped through ffmpeg.
requirements: Paper texture and grain assets, or a shader that fakes them
A font you are allowed to use for text phrases
Optional: a hosted video model API key if you want generative motion instead of scripted motion
whatYouLose: Several tuned presets instead of the one you managed to make look decent
Someone else's motion design taste on easing, parallax depth, and layer timing
Generative motion on arbitrary photos, if that is what the hosted version is actually doing
Export settings that already handle GIF dithering, loop points, and social aspect ratios without you fiddling
Fast renders on someone else's hardware instead of your laptop fans
moatNotes: The defensible part is the preset library, not the pipeline. Anyone can composite layers; making paper look like paper in motion is art direction.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the output is the whole point and nobody grades you on the pipeline. People buying this want a paper-cutout clip for a post in two minutes, and the hosted version has already made a hundred small decisions about shadow softness, fold geometry, and how fast a cutout should swing before it reads as fake. A self-built version renders fine and looks slightly wrong, and slightly wrong is the one failure mode that matters for a visual effect. Unlimited local renders only beat a credit pack if you are producing these constantly.
notes: Clone the pipeline in an afternoon, then spend the weekend discovering that paper texture is a design problem, not a code problem.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user web tool called papercut that turns a still image or a short phrase into a paper-craft style animated clip, exported as MP4 and GIF.

Stack, no substitutions: Vite + React + TypeScript for the UI, a small Node 20 Express server for rendering, HTML canvas 2D for the animation, ffmpeg via fluent-ffmpeg for encoding. No database, no accounts, no auth, no telemetry, no cloud storage. Everything runs on localhost and writes to ./out.

In scope:
- Input panel: drop or pick a PNG/JPG, or type a phrase of up to 40 characters. Pick aspect ratio 1:1, 9:16, or 16:9. Pick duration 2 to 6 seconds.
- Three presets, implemented as data-driven layer scripts, not hardcoded one-offs: "cutout-stack" (subject cut out and floating above a paper backdrop with parallax drift), "fold-reveal" (a paper fold unfolds to reveal the image), "confetti-type" (text letters as paper chips that flutter into place).
- The paper look: load a tiling paper grain texture from ./assets, draw soft offset drop shadows under every layer, add a subtle warm paper tint and a torn-edge mask generated from procedural noise. Keep these as tunable constants in one file called look.ts so they can be art-directed later.
- For image inputs, cut the subject out with a simple local approach: alpha channel if present, otherwise a flood-fill background removal with an adjustable tolerance slider. Do not pretend this is a perfect matte; show the mask preview so the user can fix the tolerance.
- Render path: the server replays the same animation script offscreen frame by frame at 30fps using node-canvas, writes PNG frames to a temp dir, then encodes MP4 (h264, yuv420p) and GIF (palettegen + paletteuse, loop forever). Delete the frames after.
- UI shows a live canvas preview with a scrub bar before you commit to a render, plus a render button with a progress readout.
- Export settings exposed: fps 15/24/30, GIF max width, MP4 quality preset, transparent-background PNG sequence as an optional zip.

Out of scope, do not build: generative video models, user accounts, sharing links, a template marketplace, watermarks, mobile apps.

If you want an optional generative mode, gate it behind a REPLICATE_API_TOKEN read from .env and default it off. Ship a .env.example, never commit secrets.

Deliver: README with setup in under five commands, npm run dev that starts UI and server together, and one example render committed to ./examples so I can see the look immediately. Tell me plainly in the README which parts of the paper look are faked and where they break.
